:question/id #uuid "22939b6a-86a1-5a24-b491-90aeb5c6c381"] ["question-22939b6a-86a1-5a24-b491-90aeb5c6c381" :question/math-academy-id "q-83475"] ["question-22939b6a-86a1-5a24-b491-90aeb5c6c381" :question/problem "![](images/85/856b131ba85b8fd1da0050ead917d5757b4b4eea46aca54bef7d7b103a896bc6.png)

Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+1$ on the closed region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\le 0,\,y\ge 0,\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 4\},$ shown above."] ["question-22939b6a-86a1-5a24-b491-90aeb5c6c381" :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To determine the critical points, we solve  ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}2x,\,-2y\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2x=0 \\ -2y=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}x=0 \\ y=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(0,0).$ Since the point $(0,0)$ does not belong to the interior of $D,$ we do not yet include it in the list of candidates for extrema (it lies on the boundary of $D,$ so we will consider it in the next step).

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the points on the boundary that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize each part of the boundary:

- The line connecting $(-2,0)$ and $(0,0)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨t,0⟩,\,t\in (-2,0).
$$

The values of $f$ on this boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,0) \\  & =(t)^{2}-(0)^{2}+1 \\  & ={t}^{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (-2,0),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ({t}^{2}+1)^{′} & =0 \\ 2t & =0 \\ t & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solution $t=0$ is not inside the interval $t\in (-2,0).$

- The line connecting $(0,0)$ and $(0,2)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨0,t⟩,\,t\in (0,2).
$$

The values of $f$ on this boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(0,t) \\  & =(0)^{2}-(t)^{2}+1 \\  & =1-{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,2),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (1-{t}^{2})^{′} & =0 \\ -2t & =0 \\ t & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solution $t=0$ is not inside the interval $t\in (0,2).$

- The quarter-circle connecting $(-2,0)$ and $(0,2)$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨t,\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}⟩,\,t\in (-2,0).\end{aligned}
$$

The values of $f$ on this boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}) \\  & ={t}^{2}-(\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}})^{2}+1 \\  & =2{t}^{2}-3.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (-2,0),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (2{t}^{2}-3)^{′} & =0 \\ 4t & =0 \\ t & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solution, $t=0$ is not inside the interval $t\in (-2,0).$

Also, we have to include the corner points of the region as candidates for extrema. So, we obtain three candidates on the boundary:

$$
(-2,0),\,(0,0),\,(0,2)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(-2,0)$ | $(0,2)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $1$ | $5$ | $-3$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-3$ at the points $(0,2),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $5$ at the point $(-2,0).$"] ["question-22939b6a-86a1-5a24-b491-90aeb5c6c381" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)=2x{y}^{2}$ on the closed region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\ge 0,\,y\ge 0,\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 4\},$ shown above."] ["question-e240afca-8d54-5fc1-a704-b3948ecfdb13" :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To determine the critical points, we solve ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2},\,4xy\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2}=0 \\ 4xy=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}x=R \\ y=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the entire segment of solutions $\{(x,0)\,:\,x\in [0,2]\}.$ Since all these points do not belong to the interior of $D,$ we do not yet include them in the list of candidates for extrema (they lie on the boundary of $D,$ so we will consider them in the next step).

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the points on the boundary that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize each part of the boundary:

- The line connecting $(0,0)$ and $(2,0)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨t,0⟩,\,t\in (0,2).
$$

The values of $f$ on this boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,0) \\  & =2(t)(0)^{2} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $F(t)$ is constant. So, $F(t)$ does not have local extremum points on the open interval $t\in (0,2).$

- The line connecting $(0,0)$ and $(0,2)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨0,t⟩,\,t\in (0,2).
$$

The values of $f$ on this boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(0,t) \\  & =2(0)(t)^{2} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $F(t)$ is constant. So, $F(t)$ does not have local extremum points on the open interval $t\in (0,2).$

- The quarter-circle connecting $(0,2)$ and $(2,0)$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨t,\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}⟩,\,t\in (0,2).\end{aligned}
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}) \\  & =2(t)(\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}})^{2} \\  & =8t-2{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,2),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (8t-2{t}^{3})^{′} & =0 \\ 8-6{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 2(4-3{t}^{2}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation gives one solution, $t=\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3},$ inside the interval $t\in (0,2).$
Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain one  candidate point, $(\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3},\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{3}).$

Also, we have to include the corner points of the region as candidates for extrema. So, in total we obtain four candidates:

$$
(0,0),\,(2,0),\,(0,2),\,(\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3},\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{3})
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(2,0)$ | $(0,2)$ | $(\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3},\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{3})$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $\frac{32\sqrt{3}}{9}$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $0$ at the points on the line segment connecting $(0,0)$ and $(2,0),$ and on the line segment connecting $(0,0)$ and $(0,2),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $\frac{32\sqrt{3}}{9}$ at the point $(\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3},\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{3}).$"] ["question-e240afca-8d54-5fc1-a704-b3948ecfdb13" :question/difficulty "question-e240afca-8d54-5fc1-a704-b3948ecfdb13"] [17592186284579 :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To determine the critical points, we solve ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}1-y & 1-x\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}1-y=0 \\ 1-x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ y=1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(1,1).$ Since the point $(1,1)$ does not belong to the interior of $D,$ we do not yet include it in the list of candidates for extrema (it lies on the boundary of $D,$ so we will consider it in the next step).

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the points on the boundary that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize each part of the boundary:

- The line connecting $(0,0)$ and $(1,0)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨t,0⟩,\,t\in (0,1).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,0) \\  & =t+0-t(0) \\  & =t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the derivative of $F(t)$ is constant. So, $F(t)$ does not have critical points on the open interval $t\in (0,1).$

- The line connecting $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨0,0⟩+t(⟨1,1⟩-⟨0,0⟩) \\  & =⟨0,0⟩+t⟨1,1⟩ \\  & =⟨t,t⟩,\,t\in (0,1).\end{aligned}
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,t) \\  & =t+t-{t}^{2} \\  & =2t-{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,1),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (2t-{t}^{2})^{′} & =0 \\ 2-2t & =0 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t=1$ does not belong to the range $t\in (0,1),$ we do not include the corresponding point in the list of candidates for extrema.

- The line connecting $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,t⟩,\,t\in (0,1).\end{aligned}
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(1,t) \\  & =1+t-t \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $F(t)$ is constant. So, $F(t)$ does not have local extremum points on the open interval $t\in (0,1).$

Also, we have to include the corner points of the region as candidates for extrema. So, in total, we obtain three candidates:

$$
(0,0),\,(1,0),\,(1,1)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(1,0)$ | $(1,1)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $0$ | $1$ | $1$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $0$ at the point $(0,0),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $1$ at the points $(1,0)$ and $(1,1).$"] [17592186125892 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the **global maximum** and **global minimum** of a function $f(x,y).$ Recall that the global maximum and minimum of a function are collectively known as **global extrema.** 

The procedure we will describe for finding the global extrema is based on a general principle called the **extreme-value theorem,** which states the following:

*Every function that is continuous on a closed, bounded region $D$ has global extrema (i.e., both a global maximum and a global minimum) on $D$*.

Let's consider the function $f(x,y) =  e^{x^2- y^2}$ on the closed  region $D=\{(x,y)\in \mathbb R^2: \,  x^2 +y^2  \leq 1\}.$ How do we find the global extrema?

To find the global extrema of a differentiable function on a closed, bounded region $D,$ we follow these steps:

**Step 1**:  Determine the critical points of $f$ in the interior of $D.$

![](images/50/5057a4a96daa4819a70e733519c89802c28bde184183db2b4efbe69d3db36e56.png)

The procedure we will describe for finding the global extrema is based on a general principle called the **extreme-value theorem,** which states the following:

> *Every function that is continuous on a closed, bounded region $D$ has global extrema (i.e., both a global maximum and a global minimum) on $D$*.

Let's consider the function $f(x,y) =  e^{x^2- y^2}$ on the closed  region $D=\{(x,y)\in \mathbb R^2: \,  x^2 +y^2  \leq 1\}.$ How do we find the global extrema?

To find the global extrema of a differentiable function on a closed, bounded region $D,$ we follow these steps:

**Step 1**:  Determine the critical points of $f$ in the interior of $D.$

![](images/50/5057a4a96daa4819a70e733519c89802c28bde184183db2b4efbe69d3db36e56.png)

To determine the critical points, we solve $\boldsymbol f' = \mathbf 0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
[\begin{aligned}2x{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} & -2y{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2x{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}=0 \\ -2y{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}x=0 \\ y=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

This gives us a single point $(0,0).$ Since the point $(0,0)$ is in the interior of $D,$ we include it in the list of candidates for extrema.

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of ${D}$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle $x^2 + y^2 =1.$ This gives

$$
\mathbf{r} = \langle \cos{t}, \sin{t} \rangle, \qquad t \in [0,2\pi).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(\operatorname{cos}t,\operatorname{sin}t) \\  & ={e}^{{cos}^{2}t-{sin}^{2}t} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}(2t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t \in (0,2\pi),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{'}(t) & =0 \\ ({e}^{\operatorname{cos}(2t)})^{'} & =0 \\ -2\operatorname{sin}(2t){e}^{\operatorname{cos}(2t)} & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}(2t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has three solutions, namely 

$$
t =\dfrac\pi 2, \: \pi, \: \dfrac{3\pi}2 \in (0,2\pi).
$$

We also have to check the endpoint of the interval, namely, $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can give rise to extreme values are 

$$
t=0, \: \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \:  \pi, \: \dfrac{3\pi}{2}.
$$

Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ for each value of $t$, we obtain the following candidate points:

$$
(1,0), \: (0,1), \: (-1,0), \: (0,-1)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values.

Evaluating $f$ at the five points we've found gives the following table of values:

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(1,0)$ | $(0,1)$ | $(-1,0)$ | $(0,-1)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $1$ | $e$ | $1/e$ | $e$ | $1/e$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $\dfrac1e$ at the points $(0,1), \, (0,-1),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $e$ at the points $(1,0), \, (-1,0).$"]]}

You are given that $f$ has a critical point at $(0.5,-0.5),$ and on the boundary of the region the points that could give rise to extreme values are $(0.5,1),$ $(0,0),$ $(0,1),$ and $(1,1).$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$  

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points inside the region $D.$ 

To determine the critical points, let's first sketch the region: 

![](images/a4/a45fd135e45e9b40d06c217e9834923ea4f70809a26e020a8d3900e8fa0a0c22.png)

Since the critical point $\left(0.5,-0.5\right)$ does not lie inside $D,$ we do not include that point in the list of candidates for the extrema.   

**Step 2.** Find the points on the boundary that could give rise to extreme values.

In this case, we are *given* the points on the boundary of our region that could potentially be global extrema for $f.$ These are

$$
\left(0.5,1\right), \quad (0,0), \quad (0,1), \quad (1,1).
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0.5,1) & ={(0.5)}^{2}-{1}^{2}-0.5-1 \\  & =0.25-2.5 \\  & =-2.25 \\ f(0,0) & ={0}^{2}-{0}^{2}-0-0 \\  & =0 \\ f(0,1) & ={0}^{2}-{1}^{2}-0-1 \\  & =-2 \\ f(1,1) & ={1}^{2}-{1}^{2}-1-1 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-2.25$ at the point $\left(0.5,1\right),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $0$ at the point $(0,0).$"} {:db/id 17592186048162} {:db/id 17592186048621} {:db/id 17592186125033 :question/id #uuid "fc6c7d4b-ed06-5426-80f2-415a147181e1" :question/math-academy-id "q-37149" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124656 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e38cefde-a663-56de-a81d-dcea6fed89b3" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Global Maxima and Minima Given the Critical Points Inside the Function's Domain"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "93c8c1df-9d34-506c-a162-63f4dc34ac81" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$f_{min} =-50$ and $f_{max} = 20$" :db/id 17592186122799} {:answer/id #uuid "08e29d0a-dfee-55a5-be4d-5ac689b1ca2c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$f_{min} = 4$ and $f_{max} = 6$" :db/id 17592186122800} {:answer/id #uuid "230b3edb-8f7e-55e8-9b01-910196f5cb4f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$f_{min} =-50$ and $f_{max} = 4$" :db/id 17592186122801} {:answer/id #uuid "678ec8d6-a00f-5ca4-9c0f-2b5c035c1955" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$f_{min} =-50$ and $f_{max} = 6$" :db/id 17592186122802} {:answer/id #uuid "7574974f-00a9-5b84-a1f0-e6e7f7ae4813" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$f_{min} =-20$ and $f_{max} = 20$" :db/id 17592186122803}] :answer-field/id #uuid "78b2ba2b-f79b-5ccd-88fe-1d78549d2f08" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186122798}] :question/problem "Find the global extrema of the function $f(x, y) = 2 + 6x - 3y + xy$ on the closed region $D$ enclosed by $y = 2x^{2}$ and $y = 8$. region $D=\big\{ (x,y) \: : \: x^2 + y^2 \leq 4 \big\}.$   You are given that the function has a critical point at $(2,0) \in D.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ that lie inside the region $D.$ 

Since the point $( 2 , 0 )$ does not belong to the interior of $D$, we do not yet include it in the list of candidates for extrema (it lies on the boundary of $D,$ so we will consider it in the next step). 

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of ${D}$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle $x^2 + y^2 =4.$ This gives

$$
\mathbf{r} = \langle 2\cos{t}, 2\sin{t} \rangle, \qquad t \in [0,2\pi).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}-4(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =4{cos}^{2}⁡t+4{sin}^{2}⁡t-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =4({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =4-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t \in (0,2\pi),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (4-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{′} & =0 \\ 8\operatorname{sin}⁡t & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation gives one solution, $t = \pi \in (0,2\pi).$ But we also have to check the endpoint of the interval, $t=0.$ So, the only values of $t$ that can possibly give rise to extreme values are $t=0,\,\pi.$ Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain two candidate points:

$$
(2,0), \quad  (-2,0)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values.

Let's compare the values of $f(x,y)$ evaluated at each of the points mentioned above. 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,0) & =(2)^{2}+(0)^{2}-4(2) \\  & =4+0-8 \\  & =-4 \\ f(-2,0) & =(-2)^{2}+(0)^{2}-4(-2) \\  & =4+0+8 \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-4$ at the point $(2,0),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $12$ at the point $(-2,0).$"} {:db/id 17592186048385} {:db/id 17592186049672} {:db/id 17592186050722} {:db/id 17592186125035 :question/id #uuid "![](images/0c/0ce5cde24ada296d945726d9f8e2f0b85900e62e9891f7ba4e25b6c181b076aa.png)

   

Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)=x^2-2x+y^2+3$ on the closed region
${D} = \{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\: : \: x \geq 0,\, x^2 + y^2 \leq4 \},$ shown above." :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To determine the critical points, we solve $\boldsymbol{f}' = \mathbf 0.$ Computing the derivative gives

![](images/81/815ebf6434a4b776ff59fb59e5b0783162e9ee69c091ae6d0f59ca94e8cf771b.png)

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2x-2=0 \\ 2y=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ y=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(1,0).$ Since the point $(1,0)$ is in the interior of $D,$ we include it in the list of candidates for extrema.

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of ${D}$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize each part of the boundary:

- The line connecting $(0,-2)$ and $(0,2)$ can be parametrized as

$$
\mathbf{r} = \langle 0, t \rangle, \qquad t \in (-2,2).
$$

The values of $f$ on this boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(0,t) \\  & =(0)^{2}-2(0)+(t)^{2}+3 \\  & ={t}^{2}+3.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t \in (-2,2),$ we solve the following equation: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ({t}^{2}+3)^{′} & =0 \\ 2t & =0 \\ t & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solution $t=0$ is inside the interval $t \in (-2,2).$  Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on this boundary, we obtain the candidate point $(0,0).$

- The half-circle connecting $(0,-2)$ and $(0,2)$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}},t⟩,\,t\in (-2,2).\end{aligned}
$$

The values of $f$ on this boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}},t) \\  & =(\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}})^{2}-2\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}+{t}^{2}+3 \\  & =7-2\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t \in (-2,2),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (7-2\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}})^{′} & =0 \\ \frac{2t}{\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}} & =0 \\ t & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation gives the solution $t=0$ inside the interval $t\in(-2,2).$  Evaluating the corresponding values of  $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain the candidate point, $(2,0).$

Also, we have to include the corner points of the region as candidates for extrema. So, we obtain a total of four candidates on the boundary:

$$
(0,0), \quad (0,-2), \quad (2,0), \quad (0,2).
$$

 

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(1,0)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(0,-2)$ | $(2,0)$ | $(0,2)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $2$ | $3$ | $7$ | $3$ | $7$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that

$(0,0),\,(1,0),\,(1,1).$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To determine the critical points, we solve ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}1-y & 1-x\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}1-y=0 \\ 1-x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ y=1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(1,1).$ Since the point $(1,1)$ does not belong to the interior of $D,$ we do not yet include it in the list of candidates for extrema (it lies on the boundary of $D,$ so we will consider it in the next step).

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the points on the boundary that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize each part of the boundary:

- The line connecting $(0,0)$ and $(1,0)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨t,0⟩,\,t\in (0,1).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,0) \\  & =t+0-t(0) \\  & =t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the derivative of $F(t)$ is constant. So, $F(t)$ does not have critical points on the open interval $t\in (0,1).$

- The line connecting $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨0,0⟩+t(⟨1,1⟩-⟨0,0⟩) \\  & =⟨0,0⟩+t⟨1,1⟩ \\  & =⟨t,t⟩,\,t\in (0,1).\end{aligned}
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,t) \\  & =t+t-{t}^{2} \\  & =2t-{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,1),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (2t-{t}^{2})^{′} & =0 \\ 2-2t & =0 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t=1$ does not belong to the range $t\in (0,1),$ we do not include the corresponding point in the list of candidates for extrema.

- The line connecting $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,t⟩,\,t\in (0,1).\end{aligned}
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(1,t) \\  & =1+t-t \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $F(t)$ is constant. So, $F(t)$ does not have local extremum points on the open interval $t\in (0,1).$

Also, we have to include the corner points of the region as candidates for extrema. So, in total, we obtain three candidates:

$$
(0,0),\,(1,0),\,(1,1)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(1,0)$ | $(1,1)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $0$ | $1$ | $1$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $0$ at the point $(0,0),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $1$ at the points $(1,0)$ and $(1,1).$"} {:db/id 17592186351513 :question/id #uuid "87ff0227-396a-5e7e-973d-bbfb82140b50" :question/math-academy-id "q-83474"} Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)=4x-xy$ on the closed region $D={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 4-{x}^{2}},$ shown above." :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To determine the critical points, we solve ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}4-y,\,-x\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}4-y=0 \\ -x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}x=0 \\ y=4\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(0,4).$ Since the point $(0,4)$ does not belong to the interior of $D,$ we do not yet include it in the list of candidates for extrema (it lies on the boundary of $D,$ so we will consider it in the next step).

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the points on the boundary that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize each part of the boundary:

- The line connecting $(-2,0)$ and $(2,0)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨t,0⟩,\,t\in (-2,2).
$$

The values of $f$ on this boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,0) \\  & =4(t)-(t)(0) \\  & =4t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the derivative of $F(t)$ is constant. So, $F(t)$ does not have critical points in the open interval $t\in (-2,2).$

- The parabola connecting $(-2,0)$ and $(2,0)$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨t,4-{t}^{2}⟩,\,t\in (-2,2).\end{aligned}
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,4-{t}^{2}) \\  & =4(t)-(t)(4-{t}^{2}) \\  & ={t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

 
To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (-2,2),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ({t}^{3})^{′} & =0 \\ 3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ t & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation gives one solution, $t=0,$ inside the interval $t\in (-2,2).$
Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain the candidate point, $(0,4).$

Also, we have to include the corner points of the region as candidates for extrema. So, in total we obtain three candidates:

$$
(0,4),\,(2,0),\,(-2,0)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,4)$ | $(2,0)$ | $(-2,0)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $0$ | $8$ | $-8$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-8$ at the point $(-2,0)$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $8$ at the points $(2,0).$"} {:db/id 17592186399180 :question/id #uuid "97e3e680-a9e7-597f-a877-a0daf5245a87" :question/math-academy-id "q-83477"} {:db/id "a059bba1-760f-57e5-af3d-31e6c7347897" :topic/math-academy-id 1947} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125655 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125892 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the **global maximum** and **global minimum** of a function $f(x,y).$ Recall that the global maximum and minimum of a function are collectively known as **global extrema.** 

The procedure we will describe for finding the global extrema is based on a general principle called the **extreme-value theorem,** which states the following:

> *Every function that is continuous on a closed, bounded region $D$ has global extrema (i.e., both a global maximum and a global minimum) on $D$*.

Let's consider the function $f(x,y) =  e^{x^2- y^2}$ on the closed  region $D=\{(x,y)\in \mathbb R^2: \,  x^2 +y^2  \leq 1\}.$ How do we find the global extrema?

To find the global extrema of a differentiable function on a closed, bounded region $D,$ we follow these steps:

**Step 1**:  Determine the critical points of $f$ in the interior of $D.$

![](images/50/5057a4a96daa4819a70e733519c89802c28bde184183db2b4efbe69d3db36e56.png)

To determine the critical points, we solve $\boldsymbol f' = \mathbf 0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
[\begin{aligned}2x{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} & -2y{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2x{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}=0 \\ -2y{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}x=0 \\ y=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

This gives us a single point $(0,0).$ Since the point $(0,0)$ is in the interior of $D,$ we include it in the list of candidates for extrema.

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of ${D}$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle $x^2 + y^2 =1.$ This gives

$$
\mathbf{r} = \langle \cos{t}, \sin{t} \rangle, \qquad t \in [0,2\pi).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(\operatorname{cos}t,\operatorname{sin}t) \\  & ={e}^{{cos}^{2}t-{sin}^{2}t} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}(2t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t \in (0,2\pi),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{'}(t) & =0 \\ ({e}^{\operatorname{cos}(2t)})^{'} & =0 \\ -2\operatorname{sin}(2t){e}^{\operatorname{cos}(2t)} & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}(2t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has three solutions, namely 

$$
t =\dfrac\pi 2, \: \pi, \: \dfrac{3\pi}2 \in (0,2\pi).
$$

We also have to check the endpoint of the interval, namely, $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can give rise to extreme values are 

$$
t=0, \: \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \:  \pi, \: \dfrac{3\pi}{2}.
$$

Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ for each value of $t$, we obtain the following candidate points:

$$
(1,0), \: (0,1), \: (-1,0), \: (0,-1)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values.

Evaluating $f$ at the five points we've found gives the following table of values:

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(1,0)$ | $(0,1)$ | $(-1,0)$ | $(0,-1)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $1$ | $e$ | $1/e$ | $e$ | $1/e$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $\dfrac1e$ at the points $(0,1), \, (0,-1),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $e$ at the points $(1,0), \, (-1,0).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b8b379fb-f7e4-5cdb-b25a-69a6c2ae9cf2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7879 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} - $f$ attains the global maximum of $e$ at the points $(1,0), \, (-1,0).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b8b379fb-f7e4-5cdb-b25a-69a6c2ae9cf2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7879 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "85def1da-b072-51a0-ae08-591a0d352331" :step/math-academy-id 45426 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125656}} {:db/id 17592186125892 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the **global maximum** and **global minimum** of a function $f(x,y).$ Recall that the global maximum and minimum of a function are collectively known as **global extrema.**
